clusters.title: The Guardian view on Covid-19 and care homes: the inquiry’s scathing verdict must be heeded | Editorial
clusters.neutral_headline: UK government failures led to Covid spreading ‘like wildfire’...

items.title: The Guardian view on Covid-19 and care homes: the inquiry’s scathing verdict must be heeded | Editorial
items.standfirst: The government did not throw a ‘protective ring’ around social care, and vulnerable people were left exposedThe families of the 43,000 care home residents in the UK whose deaths between March 2020 and July 2022 were either caused by, or contributed to, by the Covid pandemic, have waited a long time for the official verdict on the way they were treated. The report published on Tuesday confirmed what many have been saying for a long time. In the first, panicked stages of lockdown, residents and their care workers were “something of an afterthought”. The “protective ring” around care homes referred to by Matt Hancock, the former health and care secretary, was a fiction.These are scathing judgments. What actually happened, starting in March 2020, was that about 30,000 people were discharged from hospital to care homes in order to free up beds for Covid-19 patients. Since there were not enough tests for all of them, those without symptoms were moved without being tested. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, there was no instruction to isolate newly arrived residents until the second half of April (in Scotland, this happened earlier).Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? items.title: UK government failures led to Covid spreading ‘like wildfire’ in care homes, inquiry finds
items.standfirst: Inquiry chair says failure to advise care homes to isolate people discharged from hospital was ‘significant oversight’Government failures caused Covid-19 to spread “like wildfire” among vulnerable and elderly people, and Matt Hancock’s “protective ring” around care homes did not exist, a public inquiry has found.Heather Hallett, who is leading the Covid-19 inquiry, said the care sector was an “afterthought” and rejected the former health secretary’s long-held claim that he threw a “protective ring” around care homes from the start of the pandemic, saying it was “unfounded” and the “opposite was true”.
